topics: 🛏️ Tefillin Under the Head — Rava's reason, Rabbi Yirmeya's 'between pillow and mattress', and what Rava's own bed taught
👥 Two in One Bed — Shmuel permits Shema even with one's wife, Rav Yosef objects that 'his wife is like his own flesh'
🙈 What Counts as Nakedness — buttocks, a handbreadth, a leg, a voice, hair, and how old is a 'minor'
🤧 Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi Belched, Yawned, Sneezed and Spat — reconciling his conduct with a stern baraita
🌬️ Flatulence During Prayer — the baraita Rabbi Abba said was worth the whole trip
🚶 Filthy Alleyways — Rav Huna says cover your mouth and recite; Rav Ḥisda would not obey even Rabbi Yoḥanan

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Bedrooms, Bare Skin and Filthy Streets
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 24a–24b
overview.hebrewSource: טֶפַח בָּאִשָּׁה עֶרְוָה … שׁוֹק בָּאִשָּׁה עֶרְוָה … קוֹל בָּאִשָּׁה עֶרְוָה … שֵׂעָר בָּאִשָּׁה עֶרְוָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf begins by completing Rava's ruling that tefillin may be kept under one's head at night because protecting them outweighs the indignity, and Rabbi Yirmeya locates the spot between the pillow and the mattress. It then turns to reciting Shema in bed: Shmuel permits two people sharing a bed to turn away and recite, even a husband and wife, while Rav Yosef insists only a wife is 'like his own flesh'. That leads into a string of definitions of nakedness (erva): Rav Huna on buttocks, the ages at which children count as adults, and the famous four statements that a handbreadth, a leg, a voice and hair of a woman are all erva. Amud bet reconciles Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's belching, yawning, sneezing and spitting during prayer with a baraita condemning each, records the prayer said after flatulence, and closes with the debate over whether one may recite Shema while walking through filthy alleyways.

slides.title: 🛏️ Where Do Tefillin Go at Night?
slides.subtitle: Rava rules like Shmuel despite the refutation — because whatever protects them more is preferable
rows: Halakha follows Shmuel: tefillin may be under his head even when his wife is with him
כֹּל לְנַטּוֹרִינְהוּ טְפֵי עֲדִיף — whatever protects them more is preferable, even at the cost of some deprecation
Between the pillow and the mattress
Not directly aligned with his head, but off to the side
In a pouch directly under his head
Reconciled: the bulge of the pouch protrudes outward and is not under his head
Tied them in his bed curtain
Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi
On a bench with a cloth spread over them
Sent his student to fetch tefillin from between the mattress and pillow
It was the day of his wife's immersion — he did it to teach the practical halakha

callout.label: Not every refutation is equal:
callout.text: Rav Kahana asked Rav Ashi whether Rava's 'the halakha follows Shmuel despite the refutation' extends to the bed-sharing case below. Rav Ashi: 'Were all of them woven in one act of weaving?' Where it was stated, it was stated; where it was not, it was not.

slides.title: 👥 Two People in One Bed: Can Each Turn Away and Recite Shema?
slides.subtitle: Rav Yosef son of Rav Neḥunya asks Rav Yehuda; Shmuel's answer sparks an objection

lines.speaker: Shmuel
lines.text: Two who are sleeping in one bed — this one turns his face and recites Shema, and that one turns his face and recites — even if his wife is with him.

lines.speaker: Rav Yosef
lines.text: His wife — and needless to say another person?! On the contrary: אִשְׁתּוֹ כְּגוּפוֹ, his wife is like his own flesh, so he will not have lustful thoughts; another is not like his own flesh.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: One baraita: two in one bed, each turns away and recites. Another: one sleeping with his children and household beside him may not recite unless a garment separates them — but if they are minors, it is permitted. For Rav Yosef this is easy: the first is about his wife, the second about others. But for Shmuel?

lines.speaker: Shmuel
lines.text: Does it work for Rav Yosef? The second baraita also says his household — which includes his wife — needs a garment between them! You must say that the case of a wife is a tannaitic dispute for Rav Yosef; for me too it is a tannaitic dispute, and I follow one baraita.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: 'This one turns his face' — but there are still bare buttocks! This supports Rav Huna: עֲגָבוֹת אֵין בָּהֶם מִשּׁוּם עֶרְוָה, buttocks are not nakedness. Shall we add the mishna that a woman may separate ḥalla naked because she can cover her 'face' in the ground?

lines.speaker: R. Naḥman b.Y.
lines.text: No proof: that mishna is a case where her 'face' was pressed fully into the ground so her posterior was covered too.

callout.label: How old is a minor?
callout.text: Rav Ḥisda: a girl until three years and one day, a boy until nine years and one day. Some say: eleven and a day for a girl, twelve and a day for a boy. Either way, the real line is puberty — 'Your breasts were formed and your hair was grown' (Ezekiel 16:7).

slides.title: 🙈 What Is Erva? Four Statements About a Woman
slides.subtitle: Each Amora brings a verse; the Gemara narrows Rabbi Yitzḥak to one's own wife and Shema

boxes.title: Not nakedness
items: Rav Huna: buttocks are not erva
Rav Mari asked Rav Pappa about pubic hair protruding from a garment; Rav Pappa dismissed it — 'a hair, a hair', you are splitting hairs

boxes.title: A handbreadth (Rabbi Yitzḥak)
items: Not about gazing — Rav Sheshet already taught that the list of jewelry in Numbers 31:50 means whoever gazes at a woman's little finger is as if he gazed at her genitals
Rather: even his own wife, and with regard to reciting Shema

boxes.title: Leg, voice, hair
items: Rav Ḥisda: a leg is erva — 'Uncover the leg, pass through the rivers' followed by 'your nakedness shall be revealed' (Isaiah 47:2–3)
Shmuel: a voice is erva — 'For your voice is sweet and your countenance alluring' (Song of Songs 2:14)
Rav Sheshet: hair is erva — 'Your hair is like a flock of goats' (Song of Songs 4:1)

callout.label: Hanging tefillin:
callout.text: Rabbi Ḥanina saw Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi hang his tefillin, though a baraita warns that one who hangs his tefillin will have his life hang in the balance (Deuteronomy 28:66). Either he hung them by the box, not the strap — or both are forbidden and Rabbi hung them in their pouch, teaching that tefillin need not be laid flat like a Torah scroll.

slides.title: 🤧 Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi Belched, Yawned, Sneezed and Spat in Prayer
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Ḥanina's report versus a baraita that condemns all four

nodes.content: 👀 Rabbi Ḥanina: I saw Rabbi belch, yawn, sneeze, spit, and feel for a louse in his garment while praying — but he would not wrap himself in his fallen prayer shawl, and when he yawned he put his hand on his chin

❓ Baraita: sounding one's voice — little faith; raising it — like the false prophets; belching and yawning — uncouth; sneezing — a bad omen (some say: clearly repulsive); spitting — like spitting before the king

columns.label: Belch / yawn
columns.content: Rabbi did so involuntarily (לְאוֹנְסוֹ); the baraita condemns doing it deliberately

columns.label: Sneeze
columns.content: Rabbi sneezed from above; the bad omen is from below. Rav Zeira: 'One who sneezes in prayer — a good omen; as they give him relief below, so above' — worth all my learning

columns.label: Spit
columns.content: Rav Yehuda: absorb it in your garment, or in your head covering if the garment is fine. Ravina spat behind him instead: 'I am delicate'

nodes.content: ✅ Rav Huna on the voice: only one who can concentrate silently is of little faith; if he cannot, he may sound his voice — but not in a congregation, where he would disturb others

callout.label: Rabbi Abba's baraita:
callout.text: While quietly avoiding Rav Yehuda (who held that ascending from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael violates Jeremiah 27:22), Rabbi Abba heard this taught: one who breaks wind in prayer waits until the odor dissipates and resumes; some say he steps back four cubits and says, 'Master of the universe, You formed us with orifices and cavities; our disgrace and shame are revealed before You…' and resumes where he stopped. Rabbi Abba: had I come only for this, it would have been enough.

slides.title: 🚶 Walking Through Filthy Alleyways: Recite or Stop?
slides.subtitle: A lenient tradition, a fierce dissent, and verses for both outcomes

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan (some say Rabba bar bar Ḥana in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi): walking through filthy alleyways, place your hand over your mouth and recite Shema
2️⃣ Rav Ḥisda: 'By God! Had Rabbi Yoḥanan said it to me with his own mouth, I would not obey him'
3️⃣ But Rav Huna also said a Torah scholar may not stand in a place of filth, since he cannot avoid Torah thoughts. Answer: standing is forbidden, walking is permitted

4️⃣ Rabbi Yoḥanan permits contemplating Torah everywhere except the bathhouse and bathroom — and when Rabbi Abbahu fell silent in a filthy alley, Rabbi Yoḥanan told him to return to the beginning if he had paused long enough to finish. Answer: 'I do not hold so; but for you, who do — return to the beginning'
5️⃣ A baraita supports Rav Huna (hand over mouth and recite) and a baraita supports Rav Ḥisda (do not recite; if already reciting, stop)

6️⃣ If he did not stop: 'I gave them statutes that were not good' (Ezekiel 20:25), 'Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity' (Isaiah 5:18), 'He has shown contempt for the word of the Lord' (Numbers 15:31). If he stopped: 'Through this matter you will prolong your days' (Deuteronomy 32:47)

callout.label: Covered below the waist:
callout.text: Baraita: one sleeping unclothed under his garment who cannot expose his head because of the cold makes a barrier with the garment at his neck and recites (some say: at his heart) — the first tanna holds that 'his heart seeing his nakedness' is permitted. Rav Huna: if his garment is tied around his waist, he may recite Shema, whether it is cloth, leather or sackcloth.

summary.principle: Shema and prayer demand a setting free of nakedness and filth — but the daf keeps drawing the line realistically: buttocks and a wife's presence are not barriers, a sneeze is not a sin, and even a filthy street is a matter of dispute.

flowSteps.content: 🛏️ Tefillin under the head: halakha like Shmuel because protection outweighs deprecation — between pillow and mattress, off to the side
👥 Two in one bed: Shmuel — turn away and recite, even with his wife; Rav Yosef — only a wife, who is 'like his own flesh'. Both concede a tannaitic dispute

columns.content: 🙈 Erva: not buttocks (Rav Huna); a handbreadth of his wife for Shema (R' Yitzḥak); leg (Rav Ḥisda), voice (Shmuel), hair (Rav Sheshet)
🤧 Rabbi's belch, yawn, sneeze and spit in prayer were involuntary, from above, or absorbed in his garment

flowSteps.content: 🚶 Filthy alleyways: Rav Huna — hand over mouth and recite while walking; Rav Ḥisda — stop. Stopping earns long life (Deut. 32:47)
🎓 Key Principle: 'Where it was stated, it was stated' — each leniency and stringency stands on its own reasoning, and one refuted ruling does not drag the others with it

quiz.q: Why does Rava rule in accordance with Shmuel that tefillin may be placed under one's head at night, even though a baraita refuted Shmuel?
o: Because the baraita was taught by Beit Shammai
Because whatever offers the tefillin more protection is preferable, even at some cost to their dignity
Because a pouch of a handbreadth creates a separate domain
Because tefillin are not worn at night in any case
quiz.e: The daf opens with Rava's reason: 'whatever protects them more is preferable.' Rabbi Yirmeya then specifies the place — between the pillow and the mattress, not directly under his head.

quiz.q: What was Rav Yosef's objection to Shmuel's ruling that two people in one bed may each turn away and recite Shema 'even with his wife'?
o: A wife is more of a problem than a stranger because of her nakedness
The phrase 'even his wife' is backwards: his wife is like his own flesh and permitted, whereas another person is not like his own flesh
One may never recite Shema in bed at all
Only minors may share a bed with one reciting Shema
quiz.e: Rav Yosef argued that 'ishto kegufo' — a man will not have lustful thoughts about his wife — so the wife is the easier case and another person the harder one, the reverse of Shmuel's phrasing.

quiz.q: Regarding which halakha does the Gemara conclude Rabbi Yitzḥak said 'an exposed handbreadth in a woman is nakedness'?
o: The prohibition of gazing at a woman
Reciting Shema in the presence of even his own wife
Separating ḥalla while unclothed
Sleeping beside minors
quiz.e: It cannot be about gazing, since Rav Sheshet already taught that gazing at a woman's little finger with impure intent is like gazing at her nakedness. So Rabbi Yitzḥak must be speaking of one's wife and the recitation of Shema.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara reconcile Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sneezing during prayer with the baraita that calls sneezing a bad omen?
o: Rabbi sneezed only between blessings
The baraita refers to a deliberate sneeze
Rabbi sneezed 'from above' (his nose), while the bad omen refers to sneezing 'from below' (flatulence)
The baraita follows a minority opinion that Rabbi rejected
quiz.e: Belching and yawning are distinguished as involuntary versus deliberate, but for sneezing the Gemara distinguishes above from below, citing Rav Zeira's tradition that a sneeze during prayer is in fact a good omen.

quiz.q: According to the baraita that supports Rav Ḥisda, what should one do if he is in the middle of reciting Shema and reaches a filthy alleyway?
o: Place his hand over his mouth and continue
Stop reciting
Recite the rest silently in his heart
Walk faster and finish
quiz.e: The baraita in accordance with Rav Ḥisda states that one walking in filthy alleyways may not recite Shema, and if he was already reciting, he stops. Rabbi Abbahu rewards him with 'through this matter you will prolong your days'.
